implementation_notes: C++20's std::atomic::wait and notify_one/notify_all give the primitives a channel needs - an atomic flag plus a condition-variable-like wait - and libstdc++'s std::counting_semaphore plus std::latch are related. The portable construction is a bounded blocking queue over std::mutex and std::condition_variable with the same two-predicates design as the C version. A hand-rolled channel (a struct with a mutex, a deque, a closed flag, and a wait-for-item method) is idiomatic C++ because the language gives you exactly the pieces. For an SPSC channel with no blocking, a ring with two std::atomic<size_t> indices (acquire/release) is the zero-allocation form. Note the lost-wakeup hazard with atomic::wait: if the value changes between the load and the wait, the waiter sleeps - so the state must be an explicit sequence or generation counter, not a bare flag, or a notification is missed.
idiom_name: bounded queue over std::mutex + std::condition_variable (two predicates), or an SPSC ring with two atomic<size_t> indices
pitfalls: Wait on a predicate (an atomic::wait on a bare flag can miss a change between the load and the wait - a lost wakeup); use a generation counter or a condition_variable with a predicate.
notify_all on close, not notify_one, or waiting receivers are not woken.
Sending on a closed channel must be a defined no-op or an error; an unchecked send-after-close is a use-after-free of the contract.
A hand-rolled channel with an unbounded internal deque is not a bounded channel - the capacity (and the backpressure) is the point.
std::atomic::wait/notify are C++20; on C++17 use condition_variable (which is also harder to get the predicate right with).
